title: EU NIS2 Directive
hook: Europe's baseline cyber-risk rules for essential and important entities.
summary: NIS2 raises cybersecurity requirements across 18 critical sectors and strengthens incident reporting and management accountability. It applies to essential and important entities, including many suppliers that previously fell outside NIS1.
keyPoints: Eighteen sectors are covered, with essential and important entity classifications.
Management bodies are accountable for risk-management measures and must receive training.
Minimum measures cover risk analysis, incident handling, business continuity, supply chain, vulnerability disclosure, encryption, MFA and awareness.
Incident reporting requires an early warning within 24 hours, a notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month.
Supply-chain security and provider assessments are explicit obligations.
Member States transpose the directive and set supervisory regimes and fines.
Registration and cooperation with authorities depend on the entity classification.
crownJewels: Essential and important services and their supporting OT/IT.
Management decisions, risk assessments and training records.
Incident data, notifications and communication records.
clientUse: Determine entity classification and the applicable national law.
Map the minimum measures to the client's existing framework.
Build a 24/72-hour incident-reporting workflow and test it.
Brief management on their personal accountability and training duties.

title: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
hook: Operational resilience rules for the EU financial sector.
summary: DORA requires financial entities and their critical ICT providers to manage technology risk, report incidents, test resilience and govern third-party dependencies. It applies from January 2025 and shifts the focus from compliance to operational capability.
keyPoints: Five pillars: ICT risk management, incident management and reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk and information sharing.
The management body is accountable for the digital operational resilience strategy.
ICT-related incidents must be classified and reported under detailed timelines.
Significant entities must perform threat-led penetration testing periodically.
A register of ICT third-party arrangements and contractual protections are mandatory.
Critical ICT third-party providers face an EU oversight framework.
Resilience must be demonstrated through testing, scenarios and recovery capability.
crownJewels: Critical or important business services and the ICT systems behind them.
ICT third-party providers and concentration risk.
Incident reports, testing evidence and recovery plans.
clientUse: Map critical or important business functions to ICT dependencies.
Build the ICT third-party register and contract checklist.
Test incident classification and regulatory reporting.
Plan threat-led penetration testing and scenario-based resilience tests.

title: ISO/IEC 22301:2019 Business Continuity
hook: The certifiable management system for surviving disruption.
summary: ISO/IEC 22301 specifies requirements for a business continuity management system (BCMS). It helps organizations understand critical services, set recovery objectives and maintain plans that work under real disruption.
keyPoints: Business impact analysis identifies critical products, services and dependencies.
Recovery time objectives, recovery point objectives and minimum service levels drive strategy.
Continuity strategies address people, facilities, technology, suppliers and communications.
Plans must be exercised, evaluated and improved, not just documented.
Leadership, risk assessment and performance evaluation are integral to the management system.
The standard can be certified and integrates with ISO 27001 and ISO 31000.
Crisis management, warnings and communication are explicit requirements.
crownJewels: Critical products, services and business processes.
Dependencies on people, sites, technology and suppliers.
Recovery resources, backups and alternate arrangements.
clientUse: Run a BIA before selecting recovery technology.
Set RTOs and RPOs with business owners, not IT alone.
Test plans under realistic disruption scenarios.
Integrate continuity, incident response and disaster recovery.
